1023.title: yoga nidra
1023.hook: a room of people lying flat on mats, and a teacher asks each of them for one short sentence
1023.howItsDone: In a guided yoga nidra session, people lie in shavasana while a teacher leads them through a resolve, a rotation of awareness through the body, the breath and images, then the resolve again; before a puja, a sankalpa states the time, place, person and purpose.

segments.voice: Yesterday, yoga nidra with Patanjali: even sleep is a movement of the mind.

Evening, a yoga studio, the lights low. A dozen people lie flat on their backs, arms a little away from the body, palms up. A blanket here and there. Someone's foot twitches. The teacher's voice is slow and even. Settle the body. Hear the sounds outside the room. Hear the sounds inside the room. Then comes an instruction that has nothing to do with relaxing. Make your resolve. A short sentence. Say it to yourself, three times, with feeling. Nobody else will hear it.
screen: `LIGHTS LOW. BODIES ON MATS.` → `HEAR THE SOUNDS OUTSIDE, THEN INSIDE.` → `MAKE YOUR RESOLVE.`

segments.voice: The guided form of yoga nidra was set out as a sequence by Swami Satyananda Saraswati of the Bihar School of Yoga, who says in his own book on the practice that he drew on older tantric practices of placing awareness in the body. In that book, the outline runs roughly like this. Settle the body in shavasana, the corpse pose. Make a resolve. Move awareness quickly around the body, part by part. Watch the breath. Feel pairs of opposites, heavy and light, hot and cold. Let images pass. Make the resolve again. Then come back slowly. The resolve has a Sanskrit name: sankalpa. It turned up at the start of the mantra sadhana, setting the terms of a practice, and it was at home on this path long before any studio. Before a puja, a Hindu priest or householder may make a sankalpa: a spoken statement of intention that names the time, the place, the person, and the purpose of the worship about to begin. This act is chosen, on purpose, by me, here. Satyananda carried the word into the practice, with some simple advice. Keep it short. Make it sincere. Say it at the start, while the mind is still clear, and again near the end, when the body is deeply at rest and the mind, in his account, is most receptive. So the practice isn't only lying still. It opens and closes with an intention, the way a puja does. Rest becomes something you walk into on purpose.
screen: `A SEQUENCE SHAPED AT THE BIHAR SCHOOL.` · `BODY, BREATH, OPPOSITES, IMAGES.` · `SANKALPA: THE RESOLVE BEFORE A PUJA.` · `SHORT, SINCERE, AT START AND END.` · then, large: `REST, WALKED INTO ON PURPOSE.`

segments.voice: Lie down, palms up, or sit back with the hands open, and hear the sounds furthest away, then the sounds in the room, then the breath. Let a short sentence form, something true you'd like to grow into, simple and in the present, and say it to yourself three times, unhurried. Then rest in the weight of the body, and near the end, if you like, say it once more.
Yoga nidra. The sleep of yoga, which in its guided form opens and closes with a sankalpa, a short, sincere resolve.
Your line: a short, sincere resolve. The same word that opens a puja. Until tomorrow.

1024.title: yoga nidra
1024.hook: at sunset the sun's rays gather back into the sun, and an Upanishad says the senses do the same at night
1024.carry: the rays gather into the sun
1024.howItsDone: In guided yoga nidra, the teacher names parts of the body in a set order and listeners place attention on each without moving; teachers describe this rotation of awareness as a doorway to pratyahara, the withdrawal of the senses.

segments.voice: Yesterday, yoga nidra and the sankalpa: a short, sincere resolve, said at the start and the end.

A student sits before a sage and asks a question about the body at night. When a person sleeps, what is it in them that sleeps? And what stays awake? The sage, Pippalada, answers with the evening sky. At sunset, he says, the rays of the sun all gather back into that one disc of light. At sunrise they spread out again. That's what happens to the senses every night.
screen: `WHAT SLEEPS? WHAT STAYS AWAKE?` → `THE RAYS GATHER INTO THE SUN.` → `THE SENSES GATHER IN.`

segments.voice: In the Prashna Upanishad's fourth question, a student named Gargya asks this, and Pippalada's answer, in paraphrase, is this: as the rays of the setting sun become one in its disc of light, so in sleep all the senses become one in the mind, the highest of them. Then the person doesn't hear, doesn't see, doesn't smell or taste or touch, doesn't speak or take hold or move. And people say, he sleeps. Yet the breaths, the text says, keep watch in the city of the body, like fires kept burning in a house. So sleep, here, is a gathering in. Patanjali has a name for gathering in on purpose, while awake. In the second chapter of the Yoga Sutras he calls it pratyahara: the senses withdrawing from their objects and following the mind inward. The Gita gives the picture: a tortoise drawing in its limbs. Satyananda describes yoga nidra as a way into pratyahara, and the main tool is a quick tour of the body called the rotation of awareness. The guide names a part, the right-hand thumb, the second finger, the third, the palm, the wrist, and the listener simply places attention there, without moving. Then the next part. The sense of the body begins to quiet, and the outside world thins. It looks like doing very little. But it's the senses being gathered back into the mind, the way the Upanishad saw the rays gathered into the sun, only this time on purpose.
screen: `THE SENSES BECOME ONE IN THE MIND.` · `THE BREATHS KEEP WATCH, LIKE FIRES.` · `PRATYAHARA: THE SENSES DRAWN IN.` · `ATTENTION TOURS THE BODY, PART BY PART.` · then, large: `THE RAYS GATHER INTO THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Lie down or sit back with eyes closed, and without moving, let attention go where it's named: right-hand thumb, second finger, third, fourth, fifth, palm, back of the hand, wrist, elbow, shoulder, right side of the chest, right hip, knee, ankle, right big toe. Now the whole right side, all at once. Then let attention rest on the breath, keeping watch, like a fire kept burning in a house.
Yoga nidra. The sleep of yoga, where the senses gather into the mind, like rays into the setting sun, this time on purpose.
Your line: the rays gather into the sun. Tomorrow, the one who stays awake. That's day one thousand twenty-four.

1025.title: yoga nidra
1025.hook: the Katha Upanishad speaks of one who stays awake in those who sleep
1025.howItsDone: Hindus who study Vedanta speak of the sakshi, the witness that remains through waking, dream and deep sleep; teachers of yoga nidra describe the practice as deep rest for the body with awareness kept awake.

segments.voice: Yesterday, yoga nidra and the gathering in: the senses drawn into the mind, as the rays gather into the sun.
screen: `YOGA NIDRA.` · `THE RAYS GATHER INTO THE SUN.`

segments.voice: A night nurse walks a quiet ward at three in the morning. Every bed holds a sleeper. Some breathe slowly. One talks in a dream. One turns over and pulls the blanket up. The nurse is the only one awake, moving from bed to bed, seeing it all, waking no one. The Katha Upanishad has a line that sounds like that ward, but it's describing something inside each sleeper. It says someone stays awake in us while we sleep.
screen: `A QUIET WARD AT THREE A.M.` → `EVERY BED HOLDS A SLEEPER.` → `ONE IS AWAKE, WAKING NO ONE.`

segments.voice: The Katha Upanishad is Death's teaching to a boy named Nachiketas, and in its fifth section comes this, in paraphrase. The Person who is awake in those who sleep, shaping one desire after another, that is the bright one, that is Brahman, that alone is called the deathless. In the Upanishad's picture, even while we dream, while the mind builds its chariots and roads, something is awake and doing the shaping. The Gita picks up the same image and turns it around. What is night for all beings, Krishna says in chapter two, in that the self-mastered one is awake. And where beings are awake, that is night for the sage who sees. The world's busy daytime is a kind of sleep, and what the world sleeps through, the sage is awake to. Another Upanishad has a word for this one who watches: sakshi, the witness. The Shvetashvatara calls the one God, hidden in all beings, the witness, the one who knows, alone, beyond the qualities. That's where the yoga nidra days have been heading. The Goddess holding Vishnu's sleep. The Mandukya's rooms and the fourth. The falcon going home. Patanjali calling sleep a movement of the mind. The resolve. The senses gathered in. Read side by side, each can be taken, from a different angle, as pointing toward one thing: rest so deep it looks like sleep, with the witness still awake. Teachers of the practice say it plainly: the body sleeps, and awareness doesn't. Whether that's reached in one session or in a lifetime, the texts set the watcher at the center.
screen: `AWAKE IN THOSE WHO SLEEP.` · `NIGHT FOR ALL BEINGS; THE SAGE IS AWAKE.` · `SAKSHI: THE WITNESS.` · `EVERY ANGLE, ONE WATCHER.` · then, large: `THE BODY SLEEPS. AWARENESS DOESN'T.`

segments.voice: Lie down or sit back, eyes closed, and let the body go heavy, one part at a time, while the breath does what it does. Then notice that something is noticing all this: the heaviness, the breath, a sound in the room, a stray thought. Don't try to find the noticer or picture it; just rest as the one who sees, like the nurse on the ward, waking no one.
Yoga nidra. The sleep of yoga. Deep rest for the body, with the witness, the sakshi, still awake.
Your line: something in you stays awake. Tomorrow, the eyes open, on a single flame. Sleep well tonight.

1026.title: trataka
1026.hook: a candle on a low table, a dark room, and someone trying not to blink
1026.howItsDone: Practitioners of hatha yoga do trataka by gazing steadily at a small point, often a candle flame at eye level in a dark room, then closing the eyes to hold the after-image; teachers advise against gazing at the sun.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed yoga nidra with the watcher, the one awake in those who sleep. Today the eyes open.

A candle on a low table. The room is dark except for that one flame, about an arm's length away, level with the eyes. Someone sits in front of it, very still, looking. Not around it. At it. The flame leans, straightens, leans. The eyes start to sting, then water. A tear runs down one cheek and the person still doesn't look away. This isn't a staring contest. It's a practice, written down in a manual of hatha yoga, and it has a name: today's word.
screen: `ONE FLAME IN A DARK ROOM.` → `LOOKING AT IT, NOT AROUND IT.` → `UNTIL THE TEARS COME.`

segments.voice: The Hatha Yoga Pradipika lists six cleansing acts in its second chapter, and trataka is one of them. In paraphrase: with a still mind, gaze with fixed eyes at a small mark, until tears come. The teachers, it says, call this trataka. So in the text it isn't a candle exactly. It's a small point. A candle flame is one of the marks practitioners now use, and a dot on a wall is another. Then the text says what trataka does, in its own terms: it removes diseases of the eyes and drives away sloth, the heavy dullness that settles on a mind. And it adds a curious instruction: trataka should be guarded carefully, kept secret, like a casket of gold. Notice where it sits: with the cleansing acts, practices of washing and clearing the body. Trataka cleans with attention. The eye, which spends the day darting from screen to face to sign, is asked to do one thing and stay. And that's the turn from last week. Yoga nidra lay down, closed the eyes, and drew the senses in. Trataka sits up and keeps the eyes open. It uses sight, a sense that pulls hard outward, and asks it to hold still on one small point until the mind holds still behind it. A word of care: teachers advise against staring at the sun or anything harsh, and say to blink when the eyes ask. The text's tears are a sign of the gaze held, not a goal to strain for.
screen: `ONE OF SIX CLEANSING ACTS.` · `A STILL GAZE AT A SMALL MARK, UNTIL TEARS.` · `KEEP IT LIKE A CASKET OF GOLD.` · `EYES OPEN, THE MIND HELD STILL.` · then, large: `CLEANING WITH ATTENTION.`

segments.voice: Choose one small point at eye level: a mark on the wall, the tip of a pen, or a candle flame if you have one safely lit, never the sun. Look at it, not around it, letting the eyes soften and stay, and blink when you need to; this is not a contest. When the eyes tire, close them and watch whatever shape stays behind the lids until it fades, then open them and look again.
Trataka. A still gaze at one small point, until the eyes water. In the Hatha Yoga Pradipika, one of the six cleansing acts.
Your line: cleaning with attention. One small point, and the eyes stay. Day one thousand twenty-six, done.

1027.title: trataka
1027.hook: a clay lamp on a windowsill lies flat when the door opens, and stands up again when it shuts
1027.carry: the flame still burns, only the flicker goes
1027.howItsDone: Some who practice trataka use a candle or ghee lamp set at eye level in a still, draft-free room, and some recall the Gita's image of a lamp in a windless place as they sit.

segments.voice: Yesterday, trataka began: cleaning with attention, a still gaze at one small mark until the eyes water.
screen: `TRATAKA.` · `A STILL GAZE AT ONE SMALL MARK.`

segments.voice: A small clay lamp sits on a windowsill, a cotton wick in a pool of oil. Someone opens the front door. A draft runs through the house, and the flame lies down sideways, thin and blue, nearly out. The door shuts. For a moment the flame shivers. Then it stands back up, tall and still, as if nothing happened. A small drama, easy to miss. The Bhagavad Gita uses that same flame to describe a mind.
screen: `A CLAY LAMP ON A WINDOWSILL.` → `THE DOOR OPENS. THE FLAME LIES DOWN.` → `THE DOOR SHUTS. IT STANDS UP.`

segments.voice: In chapter six of the Gita, Krishna describes someone sitting in meditation, and then gives a single picture. In paraphrase: as a lamp in a place without wind does not flicker, so is the mind of the yogi who has gathered it in. Notice what the verse doesn't say. It doesn't say the yogi has no mind, or that the flame goes out. The lamp is still burning, still giving light. What's gone is the flicker. Arjuna, listening, isn't convinced. A few verses later he pushes back: the mind is restless, Krishna, stubborn and strong, and holding it seems as hard as holding the wind. It's an honest complaint, and the text keeps it in. Krishna doesn't argue. He agrees the mind is hard to hold. Then he names two things that hold it: abhyasa, practice, and vairagya, letting go. Practice is coming back, again and again. Letting go is not feeding every draft that blows through. Earlier in the same chapter, Krishna puts the coming back in plain terms: wherever the restless mind wanders off, draw it back from there, and rest it again in the Self. That's why the flame suits trataka so well. The eyes rest on the very thing the Gita compares the mind to. When a thought blows through, the flame on the table may stand perfectly still while attention leans sideways. The practice is simply to notice the lean, and come back. The Gita never promises the wind will stop forever. It describes a lamp in a sheltered place, and a person who keeps coming back to it.
screen: `A LAMP WHERE NO WIND BLOWS.` · `ARJUNA: AS HARD AS HOLDING THE WIND.` · `PRACTICE, AND LETTING GO.` · `WHEREVER IT WANDERS, DRAW IT BACK.` · then, large: `THE FLAME STILL BURNS. ONLY THE FLICKER GOES.`

segments.voice: Set a candle flame safely lit, or a mark on the wall, at eye level, and let the eyes rest on it, blinking whenever you need to. Each time a sound, a plan or a memory pulls you away, notice the lean, like a flame in a draft, and come back to the point: no scolding, just return. If the eyes tire, close them for a while, then open them and look again.
Trataka. A still gaze at one small point. Today, with the Gita's lamp in a windless place, and the coming back each time the mind leans.
Your line: the flame still burns, only the flicker goes. Practice, and letting go. See you tomorrow.

1028.title: trataka
1028.hook: a child stares at a light bulb, squeezes her eyes shut, and finds a glowing shape still floating there
1028.howItsDone: Some teachers of trataka pair the open-eyed gaze at a flame with a closed-eyed phase, in which the practitioner holds the after-image in attention until it fades, then gazes again.

segments.voice: Yesterday, trataka and the Gita's lamp in a windless place: the flame still burns, only the flicker goes.

A child lies on her bed staring up at the light bulb, because someone told her not to. Then she squeezes her eyes shut. And there it is: a glowing shape floating in the dark behind her eyelids, green, then purple, drifting when she moves her eyes. She opens them, stares again, shuts them again, delighted. It's a game. In trataka, the same thing happens, and it isn't treated as a side effect. Some teachers make it the second half.
screen: `STARE AT THE LIGHT. SHUT THE EYES.` → `A GLOWING SHAPE STAYS.` → `NOT A SIDE EFFECT. THE SECOND HALF.`

segments.voice: Some teachers of trataka describe it in two parts. Outer trataka is the gaze on the flame or the mark, eyes open. Inner trataka begins when the eyes close: the image left behind is held in attention, gently, for as long as it lasts. When it fades, some teachers say to keep looking into the place where it was, or to open the eyes and gaze again. The practice moves the same object from in front of the eyes to behind them. Why bother? The Katha Upanishad has a line that names the problem the second half answers. In paraphrase: the Self-existent one pierced the openings of the senses outward, so a person looks outward, and not at the Self within. But a certain wise one, wanting the deathless, turned the eyes around and saw the Self within. Eyes turned around: that's the heart of it. The senses are made to face out, sight especially, running ahead of us all day to the next screen, the next face, the next sign. The verse doesn't blame the eyes for that. It says that's how they were made. Then it describes someone who, for once, turns them back. Trataka does this in a very literal, very small way. The outer gaze gathers attention onto one point. Then the eyelids close, and that same gathered attention points inward at an image that exists only on the inside. It isn't the Upanishad's whole vision. It's a training run: a way of feeling, for a minute, what it might mean to turn the eyes around.

segments.voice: Set a candle flame or a small, bright mark at eye level, never the sun, and gaze at it softly for a few breaths, blinking when you need to. Then close the eyes and hold the image it left behind without squinting or chasing it, noticing its color, where it drifts, how it fades. When it's gone, rest in the dark where it was for a breath or two, then open the eyes and gaze again.
Trataka. A still gaze at one small point. Today, both halves: the flame in front of the eyes, and the image held behind them.
Your line: something of it stays inside. Outer, then inner: the flame out there, the flame in here. Until tomorrow.

1029.title: trataka
1029.hook: binding the mind to one place: Patanjali's whole definition of concentration fits in a breath
1029.carry: the mind tied to one place
1029.howItsDone: In yoga traditions that follow Patanjali, trataka is taught as a training in dharana, holding attention on a single chosen object; practitioners pick a flame, a mark, a sacred image or a flower.

segments.voice: Yesterday, trataka in two halves: the flame in front of the eyes, then the image held behind them.

Binding the mind to one place. That's Patanjali's whole definition of concentration, and it fits in a single breath. Just a mind, a place, and something tying the one to the other. A calf on a rope around a post can wander, but only so far, and it keeps circling back to the post. Trataka has spent three days putting a flame, a mark, an after-image in front of the mind. Today, the name the Yoga Sutras give to what's being trained.
screen: `BINDING THE MIND TO ONE PLACE.` → `A MIND, A PLACE, A TIE.` → `WHAT IS TRATAKA TRAINING?`

segments.voice: The third chapter of the Yoga Sutras opens with dharana. In paraphrase: dharana is the binding of the mind to a place. The sutra's word for binding is bandha, tying something down. The place can be a point in the body, Vyasa's commentary says, like the navel or the tip of the nose, or an outer object. The next sutra names what grows out of it: dhyana, meditation, when the mind's attention flows toward that place without a break. So dharana is the tying, and dhyana is when the rope goes slack because the calf has stopped pulling. Trataka is dharana you can see. The place is right there on the table. When the eyes drift, the drift is visible, and so is the coming back. And what should the place be? Patanjali is generous here. In the first chapter, after offering several supports for steadying the mind, he adds one more, in paraphrase: or by meditating on whatever one finds agreeable. The flame isn't required. A mark on the wall, a picture of a deity, a flower. What matters is the tie. Now look back at this week. The sankalpa, the short resolve. The senses gathered in, like rays into the setting sun. The watcher, awake in those who sleep. Then trataka opened the eyes: the Hatha Yoga Pradipika's still gaze at a small mark, the Gita's lamp in a windless place, the eyes turned around. And today, the name for all of it: the mind, tied to one place.
screen: `DHARANA: THE MIND TIED TO A PLACE.` · `DHYANA: ATTENTION FLOWING THERE UNBROKEN.` · `WHATEVER ONE FINDS AGREEABLE.` · `THIS WEEK: RESOLVE, GATHERING, GAZE.` · then, large: `TRATAKA IS DHARANA YOU CAN SEE.`

segments.voice: Choose your place, a candle flame safely lit, a mark on the wall, a flower or a picture that matters to you, and set it at eye level. Rest the eyes on it and picture a soft rope running from your attention to that point; when the mind wanders, let it reach the end of the rope, feel the tug, and walk back. If the eyes tire, close them and keep the point in mind.
Trataka. A still gaze at one small point. Today, dharana you can see: the mind tied to one place, and walking back each time it pulls away.
Your line: the mind tied to one place. A week of resolve, gathering and gaze. That's day one thousand twenty-nine.
